lesson.title: Days of Thunder
lesson.subtitle: The weekday etymologies — Donner, Mitte, Sonne — in one calendar

hook.title: One Pantheon, Two Calendars
hook.content: English and German named the days after the SAME gods — they just split the credit differently. Monday/Montag: the moon's day, both languages. Tuesday/Dienstag: the sky-god's day — English kept his Norse name Tiw, German kept his function as lord of the thing (the assembly), and hardened his th to d on the way. Wednesday broke the pattern: English kept Woden, German gave up and said 'mid-week' (Mittwoch). Thursday/Donnerstag you know: Thor's name against his hammer-storm. Friday/Freitag: the love goddess, Frigg or Freia, spelled two ways. Sunday/Sonntag: the sun, t → z. Seven days, one Germanic calendar.

footnotes.title: Samstag, the Sabbath Spy
footnotes.content: The seventh day is the odd one: German south says Samstag — a borrowed word from Greek sambaton (Sabbath) — while the north says Sonnabend ('Sunday-eve'). The sun's day slot ended up with two names, neither of them calqued.

pattern.title: The Calendar Grid
pattern.content: Montag (moon-day) — der, like every weekday. Dienstag (the thing-god's day; th → d). Mittwoch (mid-week — Mitte + Woche, the only one without -tag). Donnerstag (thunder-day — Thor's element where English kept Thor's name). Freitag (the goddess's day). Samstag/Sonnabend (the borrowed day). Sonntag (sun-day, t → z). All weekdays are der, all capitalize, and the calendar formula you already own slots them in: Am Montag lerne ich Deutsch — 'am' is an + dem, 'on the', the dative of time wearing a contraction.
pattern.linguist_note: The Germanic weekday names are calques of the Latin planetary week (dies Lunae, dies Martis...), which is why both languages match god-for-god. Mittwoch replaced Woden deliberately: the church preferred 'mid-week' to a pagan god's name — and English is the only Germanic language that kept Woden.

exercises.prompt: Match the weekdays with their godly twins:
exercises.explanation: Same gods, same order, one shift: the languages split the naming but kept the calendar.

exercises.prompt: Which German weekday swapped its god-name for plain geography?
exercises.explanation: English kept Woden's name; German swapped it for geography. It is also the only weekday not ending in -tag.

exercises.prompt: Why do English 'Tuesday' and German 'Dienstag' both start with a T/D sound?
options: Both honor the same god (Tīwaz/Thingsus) — and th hardened to d in German
exercises.target_answer: Both honor the same god (Tīwaz/Thingsus) — and th hardened to d in German
exercises.meaning: Tuesday ↔ Dienstag: one god, two names, one shift
exercises.explanation: The same sky-god under two titles, plus the TH→D hardening — a mythological and phonological double twin.

exercises.prompt: What English weekday is the twin of 'Sonntag'?
exercises.explanation: The identical calque: the sun's day — with Sonntag shifting the sun's t to z.

summary.outcome: Name the weekdays and tell the god-story behind each pair.
summary.takeaway: One Germanic pantheon runs both calendars — moon, thing-god, Woden/mid-week, thunder, goddess, sun.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Clock & Calendar Gym — telling time both the colloquial and the formal way.

donner.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Living in English "Thursday" (Thor's/Thunder's day = Donnerstag) and Santa's reindeer "Donner and Blitzen" (Thunder and Lightning).

montag.etymology_derivation: Moon-day: both name the day after the moon — English kept the moon's name, German kept the compound with Tag. [wiktionary]

dienstag.context_phrase: Der Dienstag kommt nach dem Montag.
dienstag.etymology_derivation: Day of the same god: Tuesday is Tiw's day (Tīwaz), Dienstag is the thing-god's day (Thingsus) — two names for one sky-god, th → d included. [wiktionary]

freitag.etymology_derivation: Frigg's/Freia's day — both languages named the day for the Germanic love goddess, spelled two ways. [wiktionary]

sonntag.etymology_derivation: Sun-day — the identical calque in both languages: the sun's day, t → z in the sun. [wiktionary]

tag.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and y → g.

woche.context_phrase: Nächste Woche fahre ich nach Berlin.
woche.context_translation: Next week I travel to Berlin.

stein.context_phrase: Ein Stein liegt auf dem Weg.
stein.context_translation: A stone lies on the path.

orange.etymology_derivation: French loan in both languages (ultimately Italian arancia) — a shared loan, no shift to fake. [wiktionary]

karotte.context_phrase: Die Karotte ist orange und gesund.
karotte.context_translation: The carrot is orange and healthy.
karotte.etymology_derivation: From French carotte, Latin carōta, Greek kărōtón — the same Greco-Latin source as English carrot. [wiktionary]

genau.context_phrase: Die Uhr zeigt genau drei Uhr.
genau.context_translation: The clock shows exactly three o'clock.
genau.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hnawwaz 'close, niggardly' — archaic Old English hnēaw is the named cognate. [wiktionary]

dumm.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German tump, Old High German tumb, Proto-Germanic *dumbaz, the exact twin of English dumb; German smoothed the -mb- cluster to -mm- and kept the old meaning. [wiktionary]

badezimmer.etymology_derivation: Compound of baden and Zimmer; Bad corresponds to English bath via the th to d shift. [wiktionary]

leder.context_phrase: Meine Schuhe sind aus echtem Leder.
leder.context_translation: My shoes are made of real leather.
leder.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *leþrą (leather): English kept the ancient th, High German hardened it to d. [wiktionary]

einkauf.context_translation: The shopping was a good deal today.
einkauf.etymology_derivation: ein + Kauf (buying): the in-buy; kaufen is the German twin of English cheap — both from Latin caupo, the tradesman (Old English ceapian, to trade). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops. This gives you an instant key to dozens of core words.
th_to_d.literature_source: Documented in Joseph Wright's Historical German Grammar as the primary dental hardening of the Second Sound Shift.
